newsitem.title: USA: CRUDE BUSINESS GRINDS SLOWLY IN STEADY U.S. MARKET.
newsitem.headline: CRUDE BUSINESS GRINDS SLOWLY IN STEADY U.S. MARKET.

text.p: U.S. crude prices stagnated Monday for domestic grade barrels as both sweet and sour differentials were unchanged from Friday, traders said.
Outright benchmark prices saw September West Texas Intermediate/Cushing gain 15 cents to $19.65-75 a barrel, with the September/October spread at minus 20-15 cents.
Grade barrels traded at nearly the exact same levels pegged on Friday, causing little excitement among Gulf Coast traders.
"There really was nothing to speak of, it was dead and the fundamentals did not move anything at all," said a dealer.
Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James sold at 15 cents over the September WTI/Cushing, with Midland/WTI selling 34 cents cheaper than benchmark.
Other trades had West Texas Sour/Midland at $1.50 under WTI, steady from Friday, and Heavy Louisiana Sweet/Empire at 33 cents under level.
WTI/Cushing Postings Plus hung at $1.86 to $1.87, working off the relatively stagnant spreads.
Late in the session, the U.N. announced that the first pair of Iraqi crude contracts gained overseer approval for a total of 11.62 million barrels.
The two companies involved were thought to be Russian and French, U.N. sources said.

Traders fully expected an onslaught of Iraqi contract approvals in the coming days, allowing Baghdad to keep pace with its stated plans to export around 1.5 million barrels per day through the first 90-days of the plan.

At issue is the U.N. "oil-for-food" accord, which permits Iraq to export $2.14 billion worth of crude in order to pay Gulf War reparations and U.N. weapons inspection costs, but mainly to buy food and medicine for civilians.
Broad trade sanctions remain in place against Iraq as punishment for invading Kuwait in August 1990.
